The question of whether playing violent video games leads to aggressive behavior is one of the most debated topics in psychology, with credible research on both sides. Several high-quality studies support a link: the APA's 2015 task force found "a consistent relation between violent video game use and increases in aggressive behavior, aggressive cognitions and aggressive affect" [d1], and a large meta-analysis of 130 research reports on more than 130,000 subjects concluded that violent video game exposure "is a causal risk factor for increased aggressive thoughts and behavior" [d8]. A University of Missouri study further found that players of violent games showed reduced brain responses to violence and set louder noise blasts for opponents — a behavioral measure of aggression — compared to nonviolent game players [d6], and two APA-published studies found that even brief exposure to violent games "can temporarily increase aggressive behavior in all types of participants" [d11]. However, a substantial body of more recent, methodologically rigorous research challenges these conclusions: a 2022 study of over 2,500 active shooter-game players found "no significant effect of playing the violent video game on aggressive affect" [d9], a study of 2,008 British teenagers using objective parental reports and official game ratings found "no link between violent video games and teenage aggression" [d12], and University of York experiments with more than 3,000 participants found "no evidence to support the theory that video games make players more violent" [d13]. The APA itself reaffirmed in 2020 that while there is "a small, reliable association between violent video game use and aggressive outcomes, such as yelling and pushing," there is "insufficient scientific evidence to support a causal link between violent video games and violent behavior" [d5], and a review in Discover Magazine noted that newer, more rigorous studies are "questioning the perceived wisdom" of earlier research [d7]. The effect, where it exists, appears to be small, context-dependent, and moderated by individual and family factors [d3], and does not clearly extend to serious criminal violence [d4][d10].
